definition: LOLITA is a natural language processing system developed by Durham University between 1986 and 2000.
details: The name is an acronym for "Large-scale, Object-based, Linguistic Interactor, Translator and Analyzer". LOLITA was developed by Roberto Garigliano and colleagues between 1986 and 2000. It was designed as a general-purpose tool for processing unrestricted text that could be the basis of a wide variety of applications. At its core was a semantic network containing some 90,000 interlinked concepts. Text could be parsed and analysed then incorporated into the semantic net, where it could be reasoned about (Long and Garigliano, 1993). Fragments of the semantic net could also be rendered back to English or Spanish. Several applications were built using the system, including financial information analysers and information extraction tools for Darpa’s “Message Understanding Conference Competitions” (MUC-6 and MUC-7). The latter involved processing original Wall Street Journal articles, to perform tasks such as identifying key job changes in businesses and summarising articles. LOLITA was one of some systems worldwide to compete in all sections of the tasks. A system description and an analysis of the MUC-6 results were written by Callaghan (Callaghan, 1998). LOLITA was an early example of a substantial application written in a functional language: it consisted of around 50,000 lines of Haskell, with around 6000 lines of C. It is also a complex and demanding application, in which many aspects of Haskell were invaluable in development. LOLITA was designed to handle unrestricted text, so that ambiguity at various levels was unavoidable and significant. Laziness was essential in handling the explosion of syntactic ambiguity resulting from a large grammar, and it was much used with semantic ambiguity too. The system used multiple "domain specific embedded languages" for semantic and pragmatic processing and for generation of natural language text from the semantic net. Also, important was the ability to work with complex abstractions and to prototype new analysis algorithms quickly. Later systems based on the same design include Concepts and SenseGraph.

explainer.lead: LOLITA is a natural language processing system developed at Durham University between 1986 and 2000. It matters as an early general-purpose tool for processing unrestricted text, built around a large semantic network.

tiers.eli5: It is like a giant web of linked ideas; you feed it text, it hangs the text on the web, and then it can reason about what it has stored.
tiers.practitioner: The system parsed and analysed text, then incorporated it into a semantic net of about 90,000 interlinked concepts where it could be reasoned over. A pitfall for modern users is that it reflects its era's engineering, so it serves as historical reference rather than a current library.
tiers.paperLevel: Its name stands for Large-scale, Object-based, Linguistic Interactor, Translator and Analyzer; the core is a semantic network of roughly 90,000 interlinked concepts used for parsing, analysis and reasoning, without the scale of modern statistical methods.

explainer.example: Text is parsed and its concepts are added to the semantic net, after which queries can be answered by reasoning across the interlinked concepts.
